  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,

```{r setup}
library(multisiteDGP)
```

When the site estimates and standard errors of a completed study are at hand,
a design can be set up to resemble that study. The steps are to compute the
design values from the data, to build the design, and to compare simulated
data with the observed data. The last section builds a grid of designs around
the calibrated one.

## From observed estimates to design values

The example data are simulated once and from then on treated as the observed
data of a completed trial. Only the columns that a trial reports are kept: the
estimate, its standard error, and the site size.

```{r observed}
trial <- sim_multisite(
  J = 30, tau = 0.1, sigma_tau = 0.2,
  nj_mean = 100, cv = 0.5, nj_min = 20, R2 = 0.4, seed = 1
)
obs <- data.frame(
  tau_j_hat = trial$tau_j_hat, se_j = trial$se_j, n_j = trial$n_j
)
head(obs)
```

The number of sites is the number of rows, and the grand mean is estimated by
the mean of the estimates. The estimates vary because the site effects vary
and because each estimate has sampling error, so their variance is, on
average, $\sigma_\tau^2$ plus the mean sampling variance. Subtracting the mean
sampling variance gives a moment estimate of $\sigma_\tau^2$.

```{r moments}
se2 <- obs$se_j^2
sigma_tau_hat <- sqrt(var(obs$tau_j_hat) - mean(se2))
round(c(J = nrow(obs), tau = mean(obs$tau_j_hat), sigma_tau = sigma_tau_hat), 3)
```

The grand mean is estimated at 0.144 and the cross-site standard deviation at
0.189. The data were simulated with 0.1 and 0.2. Estimates from 30 sites are
not exact, and a design calibrated to a real study carries the same
uncertainty. A random-effects meta-analysis or a multilevel model of the same
data estimates the same two quantities and can be used instead. A negative
difference under the square root means that the estimates vary no more than
their standard errors predict. A design needs a positive `sigma_tau`, so the
value then has to come from elsewhere.

Two numbers describe the standard errors. The informativeness $I$ is the share
of $\sigma_\tau^2$ in the sum of $\sigma_\tau^2$ and the geometric mean $GM$
of the sampling variances. The heterogeneity ratio $R$ is the largest sampling
variance divided by the smallest.

```{r standard-errors}
GM <- exp(mean(log(se2)))
I_hat <- sigma_tau_hat^2 / (sigma_tau_hat^2 + GM)
R_hat <- max(se2) / min(se2)
round(c(GM = GM, I = I_hat, R = R_hat), 3)
round(c(compute_I(se2, sigma_tau = sigma_tau_hat), heterogeneity_ratio(se2)), 3)
```

The last line shows that `compute_I()` and `heterogeneity_ratio()` do the same
arithmetic. $I$ is 0.561, so a little more than half of the variance of a
typical estimate comes from the site effects, and $R$ is 5.273. Solved for the
cross-site variance, the definition of $I$ reads
$\sigma_\tau^2 = I \cdot GM / (1 - I)$. This supplies a value of `sigma_tau`
for a chosen $I$ when the moment estimate is not usable.

## Building the design

A design describes the standard errors in one of two ways. A multisite trial
reports site sizes, and `sim_multisite()` derives the standard errors from
simulated site sizes. For a study that reports only standard errors, as most
meta-analyses do, `sim_meta()` sets the standard errors directly from $I$ and
$R$. `vignette("site-sizes-and-standard-errors")` describes both.

From the site sizes the design takes the mean, the coefficient of variation,
and the minimum. It also needs `kappa`, the constant in `se2_j = kappa / n_j`.

```{r site-sizes}
n <- obs$n_j
round(c(nj_mean = mean(n), cv = sd(n) / mean(n), nj_min = min(n)), 2)
median(se2 * n)
compute_kappa(p = 0.5, R2 = 0.4)
```

The median product of sampling variance and site size is 2.4. In these
simulated data the product is the same in every site. In real data it varies,
which is why the median is used. The design has no `kappa` argument. It
computes `kappa` from the proportion treated `p`, the share `R2` of outcome
variance explained by covariates, and the outcome variance, as
`compute_kappa()` does. With half of each site treated and an outcome variance
of 1, `kappa` is `4 * (1 - R2)`, so `R2 = 0.4` reproduces the 2.4 of the data.
Only `kappa` matters for the standard errors, and any values of the three
arguments that give it will do.

```{r design}
design <- multisitedgp_design(
  J = 30, tau = 0.14, sigma_tau = 0.19,
  nj_mean = 94, cv = 0.4, nj_min = 33, R2 = 0.4
)
design
```

The design holds the values above, rounded. The arguments that are not given
keep their defaults, among them normal site effects and no dependence between
effects and precision. To describe the standard errors by $I$ and $R$
instead, set `paradigm = "direct"`. This argument of `multisitedgp_design()`
says where the standard errors come from, and its default is `"site_size"`.

```{r design-direct}
design_direct <- multisitedgp_design(
  paradigm = "direct", J = 30, tau = 0.14, sigma_tau = 0.19,
  I = 0.56, R = 5.3
)
design_direct
```

The second block now reads `I` and `R`. A preset is a third starting point.
When a publication gives only the number of sites and the cross-site standard
deviation, `preset_education_modest(J = 30, sigma_tau = 0.19)` takes those two
values and keeps the site sizes of the preset. `vignette("multisiteDGP")`
shows such overrides.

## Checking the calibration

One data set simulated from each design shows whether the design resembles
the observed data.

```{r check}
# Seed 1 would repeat the random numbers that made the example data.
sim <- sim_multisite(design, seed = 2)
sim_direct <- sim_meta(design_direct, seed = 2)
summary(sim)
c(I = informativeness(sim_direct), R = heterogeneity_ratio(sim_direct))
```

The scale block holds the values to compare with the observed data: an
informativeness of 0.579 (observed 0.561), a heterogeneity ratio of 4.692
(5.273), and a geometric mean of the sampling variances of 0.026 (0.028). The
statuses do not judge this match. They compare the simulated data set with its
own design and with fixed rules, as `vignette("multisiteDGP")` explains.
The last line belongs to `sim_direct`: `sim_meta()` reproduces the $I$ and $R$
of its design in every data set.

```{r compare, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Most standard errors lie near 0.15 in the left and middle panels and are spread evenly in the right panel."}
library(ggplot2)
cols <- c("tau_j_hat", "se_j")
panels <- rbind(
  data.frame(set = "observed", obs[cols]),
  data.frame(set = "simulated, from site sizes", sim[cols]),
  data.frame(set = "simulated, set directly", sim_direct[cols])
)
ggplot(panels, aes(tau_j_hat, se_j)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5)) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  facet_wrap(~set) +
  labs(x = "Estimate", y = "Standard error")
```

The most precise sites are at the top of each panel, and the estimates scatter
over a similar range in all three. In the observed data most sites sit in a
band of standard errors near 0.15, with a tail of less precise sites below.
The data simulated from site sizes have the same shape. `sim_meta()` spaces
the sampling variances evenly on the log scale between the smallest and the
largest, so its standard errors reproduce $I$ and $R$ and not the shape of the
observed distribution. To simulate with the observed standard errors
themselves, add the argument `se_fn = function(J) list(se2_j = se2)` to
`design_direct`.

## A grid of designs around the calibrated one

A simulation study usually runs over several designs. The calibrated design is
the base design, and a grid around it varies what is uncertain or what a new
trial would change. The cross-site standard deviation was estimated from only 30
sites, so the grid adds values of about half and one and a half times the
estimate. It also adds a trial with twice as many sites.

```{r grid}
grid <- design_grid(
  base_design = design,
  J = c(30, 60),
  sigma_tau = c(0.10, 0.19, 0.28),
  seed_root = 1
)
grid
```

Each row holds one design, a copy of the base design with two values
replaced, and a seed derived from `seed_root`. `scenario_audit()` simulates
`M` data sets from each row and summarizes their diagnostics.

```{r audit}
audit <- scenario_audit(grid, M = 50)
audit[, c("J", "sigma_tau", "med_I_hat", "med_R_hat", "q95_R_hat",
          "med_mean_shrinkage")]
```

The columns starting with `med_` are medians over the 50 data sets of a row,
and `q95_R_hat` is a 95th percentile. The second row is the base design. Its
median informativeness is 0.567 and its median heterogeneity ratio 4.70, with
a 95th percentile of 7.11, so the observed 0.561 and 5.273 are ordinary values
under this design. Informativeness follows the cross-site standard deviation,
from 0.264 at 0.10 to 0.740 at 0.28, and hardly changes with the number of
sites. The heterogeneity ratio does change. Its median rises to 5.86 in the
fifth row, because the two most extreme of 60 sites lie further apart than
those of 30. `med_mean_shrinkage` is the median of the mean shrinkage, the
average of the weights $S_j$ that a normal model puts on each site's own
estimate. Like informativeness, it follows the cross-site standard deviation,
from 0.27 at 0.10 to 0.73 at 0.28 with 30 sites, and hardly changes with the
number of sites.

`audit` has more columns than shown, among them a `status` that compares the
medians with the thresholds in `default_thresholds()`. The two designs with
`sigma_tau = 0.10` fail, because their mean shrinkage is below the threshold
of 0.30. `vignette("diagnostics-and-presets")` describes the thresholds. The
simulation study itself then draws its data sets from the designs in
`grid$design`.
